10: תרתי Why do I need two [phrases to teach] after the fact? -  The Mishna should have been taught as follows: "The slaughter of everyone is valid [after the fact], except for that of a deaf-mute, and imbecile, and a minor." [Had it done so,] it would properly be implied that those who are included in "everyone" after the fact, are included, but not [that they have the right to slaughter] ab initio. Alternatively, it should have taught, "Everyone may slaughter" separately (i.e., omitting "and their slaughter is valid"), as it is taught elsewhere, "[everyone] may make vows of valuation" and "[everyone] may vow" without [further] explaining, "Why do I need [the Mishnah] to teach this?" [Rather,] "everyone may slaughter" is necessary in order to explain "and their slaughter is valid," to say that those who [are included in] "slaughter" in the opening phrase [are only considered valid to slaughter] after the fact. And if that is difficult [for you], in Temurah it is also taught in this way, and it is explained over there. It is not taught in that case, "All may substitute, and their substitutions are [valid] substitutions," next to each other. And if it is because of, "Not that a person is permitted" (Tem. 2a:2), but in the event that one may come to engage in such a [forbidden] act, that he would be subject to forty lashes, to teach us that one is administered lashes on account of [violating] a negative commandment [even] where no physical action is [involved] in it.
